extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and graduate students in geometric analysis and Ricci flow
extracted.subtask_description: Conditions, assumptions and quantitative estimates used to construct and analyse Ricci flow with δ-cutoff surgeries on compact 3-manifolds (canonical neighborhood assumption, noncollapsing, curvature/volume bounds, surgery parameter constraints, and long-time/topological consequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pinching and canonical neighborhood assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution (with surgeries) is required to satisfy the pinching assumption and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy ε) with a scale function r = r(t) (nonincreasing, continuous positive function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One chooses nonincreasing positive functions r(t) and ¯δ(t) so that for any admissible δ(t) < ¯δ(t) the evolving solution with δ-cutoff surgeries satisfies the pinching and canonical neighborhood assumptions at all relevant times and scales. These are global structural hypotheses used repeatedly (they guarantee canonical neighborhoods at high curvature points and control geometric behaviour near surgeries).

rubrics_metrics.name: δ-cutoff surgery procedure and parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Surgeries are performed at times ti with the cutoff parameter δ = δ(ti); at each surgery a cutoff radius h(ti) (depending only on δ(ti) and r(ti)) is used and the surgery is performed deeply inside ε-horns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The surgery construction must ensure cutoffs happen in the ε-horns (so unaffected regions retain geometric control), the cutoff radius h(ti) depends only on δ(ti) and r(ti), and each cutoff decreases the volume by at least h(ti)^3. The choice of δ(t) must respect upper bounds ¯δA(t0) appearing in curvature estimates (Theorem 7.5.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surgery times cannot accumulate (discreteness of surgery times)
rubrics_metrics.description: The surgery times ti cannot accumulate in any finite time interval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because each δ-cutoff surgery removes at least h(ti)^3 volume and total volume is finite and decays (and Rmin(t) nondecreasing), the surgery times are isolated. This is used to show surgeries are discrete and to obtain long-time existence statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonicity/evolution of minimum scalar curvature and extinction criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimum scalar curvature R_min(t) of the surgically modified solution is nondecreasing and satisfies d/dt R_min(t) ≥ (2/3) R_min(t)^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular, if the initial manifold has scalar curvature bounded below by a > 0 then the solution becomes extinct in finite time (T ≤ 3/(2a)). This inequality is used both for extinction/topological conclusions and to control large-time behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-time existence alternatives (Theorem 7.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 there exist nonincreasing positive functions r(t), ¯δ(t) so that for any δ(t)<¯δ(t) the Ricci flow with δ-cutoff surgeries either (i) becomes extinct in finite time after finitely many cutoffs (and the initial manifold is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of S2×S1 and S3/Γ), or (ii) exists for all t∈[0,∞), performing at most countably many cutoffs, with at most finitely many surgeries on each finite time interval, and the pinching and canonical neighborhood assumptions (accuracy ε, scale r(t)) are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the main long-time existence theorem: the solution is obtained by evolving Ricci flow and performing δ-cutoff surgeries with δ(t) and r(t) chosen appropriately; the theorem gives two exhaustive alternatives and topological conclusions in case (i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabolic neighborhood hypotheses for local estimates (hypotheses of Theorem 7.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply the curvature/noncollapsing conclusions one assumes the solution (with surgeries) is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood P(x0,t0,r0,r0^2) (i.e. Bt(x0,r0) exists for t∈[t0−r0^2,t0]) and satisfies |Rm| ≤ r0^{−2} on that parabolic neighborhood and Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r0)) ≥ A^{-1} r0^3. Also each δ-cutoff in [t0/2,t0] must satisfy δ ≤ ¯δ_A(t0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These local hypotheses are scaling-invariant and are the starting assumptions for Theorem 7.5.1 which yields κ-noncollapsing, canonical neighborhoods at high curvature points, and local curvature upper bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsed on scales < r0 (Theorem 7.5.1 (i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.5.1 there exists κ = κ(A,ε) > 0 such that the solution is κ-noncollapsed on all scales less than r0 inside B_{t0}(x0,A r0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: κ depends only on A and ε (and the canonical neighborhood constants). The proof uses Perelman's reduced volume and control of admissible curves to avoid surgery regions. This noncollapsing holds regardless of how large the time t0 is, provided the local hypotheses hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood conclusion for high curvature points (Theorem 7.5.1 (ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists K1 = K1(A,ε) such that every point x ∈ B_{t0}(x0,A r0) with R(x,t0) ≥ K1 r0^{−2} has a canonical neighborhood B containing B_{t0}(x,σ) for some 0<σ<C1(ε) R(x,t0)^{−1/2}, and this canonical neighborhood is either a strong ε-neck or an ε-cap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C1(ε) is the constant from the canonical neighborhood assumption. This gives a precise geometric description of regions of high scalar curvature: either neck-like or cap-like, with quantified radii tied to curvature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature upper bound when r0 ≤ r̄ √t0 (Theorem 7.5.1 (iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If r0 ≤ r̄(A,ε) sqrt(t0) then there exists K2 = K2(A,ε) with R ≤ K2 r0^{−2} in B_{t0}(x0,A r0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a local curvature control: provided the base scale r0 is at most the specified fraction of sqrt(t0), the curvature in the larger ball is uniformly bounded by K2 r0^{−2}. The constants depend on A and ε.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible / barely admissible curve reduced-length lower bound (control of surgery-avoiding geodesics)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a chosen large L one can find ¯δ(L,t0,r(t0),ε)>0 so that whenever every δ-cutoff in [t0/2,t0] satisfies δ ≤ ¯δ, any barely admissible space-time curve γ (one that lies on the boundary of admissible curves) parametrized on [tγ,t0] satisfies ∫_{tγ}^{t0} (R(γ(t),t) + |γ̇(t)|^2) dt ≥ L r0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This integral lower bound forces minimizing reduced-length curves joining certain regions to stay in surgery-unaffected regions; it is a technical ingredient used to obtain reduced-volume lower bounds and hence noncollapsing. One needs to choose δ small depending on L and local data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perelman's reduced-volume lower bound implies volume noncollapsing
rubrics_metrics.description: From the parabolic hypotheses and the reduced-length control one obtains a positive lower bound for Perelman's reduced volume of a suitable cone-like subset (equation (7.5.8)), which in turn produces a uniform lower bound for Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x,ρ))/ρ^3 (i.e. noncollapsing) for small ρ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument constructs cone-like subsets of space-time formed by minimal reduced-length curves; by Jacobian comparison (Perelman's theorem) and the reduced-volume lower bound one derives explicit volume lower bounds for balls, used to prove κ-noncollapsing in the presence of surgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale relation for canonical neighborhoods (σ bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a point x has large scalar curvature R at time t0 and a canonical neighborhood B is asserted, the neighborhood contains a ball B_{t0}(x,σ) for some σ with 0 < σ < C1(ε) R^{-1/2}, tying geometric size to curvature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quantifies the canonical neighborhood size in terms of the curvature at its center: the canonical neighborhood radius is controlled by C1(ε) times the curvature radius R^{-1/2}. This relation is used to compare local scales and to bootstrap curvature/derivative estimates (Shi-type estimates) inside canonical regions.
